title: Design Uber (ride hailing)
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, estimates, geo index (geohash/quadtree/H3), matching, ETA, location ingestion, surge.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Uber matches a rider who wants a trip with a nearby driver who is free, then shows the car moving on the map and an ETA. Three hard problems hide inside: "who is near me" (a geo index), "which one should I pick" (matching), and "how long will it take" (ETA on a road graph). Lyft, Ola, Grab and Bolt are the same shape.

Functional requirements

  • Driver app sends location every few seconds while online.
  • Rider requests a trip (pickup, drop-off); the system shows price and ETA, then matches a driver.
  • Driver gets an offer and accepts or declines; rider sees the car approaching live.
  • Trip lifecycle: requested, matched, arriving, in progress, completed, paid.

Non-functional requirements

  • Match within about 5 s p95; nearby-driver query under 100 ms.
  • Location writes are huge in volume, but losing one ping is fine (the next arrives in 4 s).
  • A driver must never get two trips at once, and a trip must never get two drivers (strong consistency on the assignment only).
  • Available during peaks (Friday night, rain, New Year's Eve), city by city.

Decision gravity. Treat location (high volume, lossy, ephemeral) and trips (low volume, must be correct, durable) as two different systems with different stores. This split is cheap to make now and painful to undo later, because merging them means putting a firehose through your transactional database.

Everyday analogy. A taxi dispatcher with a big map and pins for free cabs: pins move constantly (cheap to lose), but writing a booking in the ledger must be exact.

Common interview traps.

  • Using one SQL table for both live driver positions and trips.
  • Not asking about scope: pooling, scheduled rides, surge, payments.
  • Forgetting that "nearby" must mean road distance, not straight line.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
Rider-facing REST plus a persistent connection (WebSocket or gRPC stream) for live updates.

POST /v1/trips/estimate
{ "pickup": {"lat": 12.9716, "lng": 77.5946},
  "dropoff": {"lat": 12.9352, "lng": 77.6245}, "product": "uberx" }
200 { "etaToPickupSec": 240, "distanceKm": 6.1, "fare": {"min": 180, "max": 210, "currency": "INR"},
      "surge": 1.2, "quoteId": "q_91af" }
POST /v1/trips
Idempotency-Key: 7b1c-...        // retry-safe on flaky mobile networks
{ "quoteId": "q_91af" }
202 { "tripId": "t_88213", "state": "REQUESTED" }
POST /v1/trips/t_88213/cancel     -> 200 (fee may apply after match)
GET  /v1/trips/t_88213            -> state, driver, vehicle, polyline
POST /v1/drivers/me/location        // or a streaming RPC; batch 1 ping/4s
{ "lat": 12.9716, "lng": 77.5946, "heading": 90, "speed": 8.3, "ts": 1731150000, "seq": 20991 }
204 No Content

POST /v1/offers/o_55/accept   (driver)   -> 200 | 409 already taken or expired
WS   /v1/stream  -> {"type":"driver_moved","lat":..,"lng":..} / {"type":"state","state":"ARRIVING"}

seq lets the server drop out-of-order pings. The idempotency key on trip creation is the guard against a double tap creating two trips.

Industry example. Uber's public developer APIs expose estimate, request and status endpoints of this shape; internally real-time driver location rides a long-lived connection rather than HTTP per ping.

Everyday analogy. Ordering at a counter with a numbered receipt: show the receipt twice and you still get one meal.

Common interview traps.

  • Polling every second from the rider app instead of pushing.
  • No idempotency on trip creation.
  • Letting the client claim a driver (the server decides assignment).

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 20M rides/day globally at peak design, 5M drivers online at peak, one ping per 4 s.

Quantity Calculation Result
Trip creates 20M / 86,400 about 230/s avg, peak 1,000/s
Driver pings 5M / 4 s 1.25M writes/s
Ping size id 8 B + lat/lng 16 B + ts, heading, speed ~16 B ~40 B (about 100 B on the wire with headers)
Ping bandwidth 1.25M x 100 B ~125 MB/s into the edge
Live index memory 5M drivers x ~100 B ~500 MB total (tiny!)
Nearby queries each trip asks maybe 5 times about 5,000/s peak
Trip storage 20M/day x 2 KB x 365 ~15 TB/year
Trace archive 1.25M x 40 B x 86,400 s ~4 TB/day if every ping is kept

What this tells you. The live position table is small enough for RAM; the problem is 1.25M writes/s, so shard it by city/region, not by driver. Persisting every ping forever is a choice, not a requirement: sample to 1 point per 10 s for trip history and send raw pings to cheap cold storage with a 30-day TTL.

Everyday analogy. Counting how many cabs are on the road tells you the pin board fits on a wall, but the radio chatter is relentless.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing each ping in the transactional trip DB (1M writes/s will melt it).
  • Forgetting peak versus average.
  • Computing storage for pings as if all must be queryable forever.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Location gateway: terminates millions of long-lived connections, validates, forwards pings.
  • Supply index (geo index): in-memory map of cell id to set of free drivers, sharded by city. Updated by pings.
  • Matching (dispatch) service: for a request, queries nearby supply, ranks candidates by ETA, offers sequentially or in small batches.
  • ETA service: road graph plus live traffic, returns seconds and distance.
  • Trip service: state machine in a durable DB (Postgres or MySQL sharded by city or tripId; Uber has used Cassandra and later MySQL-based Schemaless/Docstore for trips).
  • Kafka: ping and trip events feed pricing, analytics, fraud, trace storage.

Trip state machine

REQUESTED -> OFFERED -> ACCEPTED -> ARRIVING -> IN_PROGRESS -> COMPLETED
     |          |          |
  CANCELLED  EXPIRED    CANCELLED(fee)

Decision gravity. Shard everything by geography (city or cell range), because the matching question is always local. Alternative: shard by driver id, which scatters a "who is near me" query across all shards. Geography breaks at city borders and at huge hotspots (a stadium), which you handle with overlapping cells and splitting hot cells. Changing the sharding key later is a one-way door.

Industry examples. Uber's Ringpop with consistent hashing sharded dispatch ("DISCO") by geography; Uber open-sourced H3 hexagonal indexing. Lyft and Grab use geohash or S2 variants.

Everyday analogy. Regional dispatch offices that each only know about cabs in their own district.

Common interview traps.

  • A single global matching service with a global lock.
  • Not drawing the separation between location firehose and trip transactions.
  • No mention of what happens when the driver app loses connectivity.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Geo index: geohash, quadtree, S2 and H3

Question: given a point, find drivers within about 2 km, fast. A SQL WHERE sqrt(...) < 2 scans everything, so we bucket the earth into cells and look up the rider's cell plus neighbours.

  • Geohash: interleave latitude and longitude bits, base32. Same prefix means same rectangle. Precision 6 is about 1.2 km x 0.6 km. Simple, works in Redis (GEOADD/GEOSEARCH uses a geohash-encoded sorted set), but cells are rectangles with distortion near poles and the edge problem (two close points may have very different prefixes).
  • Quadtree: recursively split a cell into 4 when it holds more than N drivers. Adapts to density (dense downtown gets small cells), but needs rebalancing as drivers move.
  • S2 (Google) / H3 (Uber): spheres divided into hierarchical cells; H3 hexagons have equal-distance neighbours (ring of 6), which makes "k-ring" queries uniform. Resolution 8 is about 0.7 km^2 edge ~460 m, resolution 9 is about 175 m edge.

Update flow when a ping arrives: compute new cell; if different from old, remove from old set, add to new, in one in-memory shard operation. About 90% of pings stay in the same cell, so most are a cheap overwrite of lat/lng.

# Nearby query sketch with H3 (h3-py v3 naming, confirm for your version)
import h3
def nearby(lat, lng, k=2):
    center = h3.geo_to_h3(lat, lng, 8)
    cells = h3.k_ring(center, k)        # 19 cells for k=2
    return [d for c in cells for d in cell_to_drivers.get(c, ())]

Redis GEO vs custom. Redis GEOSEARCH ... BYRADIUS 2 km returns in about 1 ms for thousands of members, good to ~100k writes/s per node. At 1.25M/s total across regions you need many shards anyway, which is why large players write custom in-memory services (Go, C++, Java) keyed by cell.

Decision gravity. Cell scheme is a one-way door: every stored cell id and every shard boundary depends on it. H3 at resolution 8 to 9 is a common choice. Alternatives: geohash (simplest, fine for a first product), S2 (great hierarchy, square-ish). It breaks at the density extremes: choose the resolution so an average cell holds about 10 to 50 drivers, and re-split hot cells.

Everyday analogy. A city map overlaid with a grid; instead of measuring to every taxi you look at the squares around you.

Common interview traps.

  • Searching only the rider's own cell and missing a driver 10 m away in the next one.
  • Putting a persistent DB in the update path for every ping.
  • Straight-line radius ignoring rivers and one-way streets.

Matching: who gets the offer

Candidates come from the geo index (say top 10 by straight distance). Then rank by ETA to pickup, not distance, and by other factors (driver rating, acceptance rate, vehicle type, fairness/idle time).

Strategies:

  1. Greedy nearest-first, sequential offers. Offer to best driver, wait 10 to 15 s for accept, then next. Simple, but slow when drivers decline.
  2. Parallel offers to a few. First accept wins; faster, but wastes drivers' attention.
  3. Batched global optimisation. Every 2 s, collect all open requests and all free drivers in an area and solve an assignment problem (Hungarian or min-cost matching) to minimise total pickup time. Better overall ETAs than greedy, which can steal a driver from a rider who needed them more. Uber and Lyft have described batched matching.

Avoiding double booking. A driver's state lives in one place (the shard that owns that driver). Moving driver from AVAILABLE to OFFERED(tripId) is a compare-and-set on that owner. If the CAS fails, the next candidate is tried. The offer has a TTL of about 15 s after which the state auto-reverts.

-- If drivers' state were in Postgres (small scale), the same idea
UPDATE driver_state SET status='OFFERED', trip_id=$1, offer_expires=now()+interval '15 seconds'
 WHERE driver_id=$2 AND status='AVAILABLE';   -- 0 rows updated means someone else won

Decision gravity. Start greedy-sequential; move to batched matching when you have the density to benefit (it needs many riders and drivers per window). Reversible, because it is a policy change inside the matching service. The ownership of driver state by one shard is the invariant that is hard to retrofit.

Everyday analogy. A taxi rank: the dispatcher shouts a job to the front cab and a cab can only say yes to one job at a time.

Common interview traps.

  • Offers to the nearest driver by straight line when the ETA is 15 minutes because of a bridge.
  • No timeout on an offer, leaving a rider stuck.
  • Using a distributed lock service for every offer when ownership by shard is simpler.

ETA and routing

ETA to pickup and to drop-off is sum over road segments (length / predicted speed). The road map is a graph (OpenStreetMap or commercial), roughly 100M+ edges globally.

  • Shortest path: plain Dijkstra is too slow on continent-size graphs (seconds). Use contraction hierarchies or A* with landmarks, preprocessing the graph once so a query takes under 1 ms to a few ms.
  • Live traffic: probe data from your own drivers' pings, map-matched to segments, aggregated into median speed per segment per 5 minutes; combine with historical speed by hour of week.
  • ML correction: a model (gradient boosted trees or neural net) predicts the residual error of the routing ETA using time, weather, region. Uber has described such an ETA post-processing model.
  • Cache: ETA between two H3 cells at the same hour changes slowly, so cache (origin cell, dest cell, time bucket) -> seconds for 1 to 5 minutes for coarse estimates (price quote), and compute exact only for the final few candidates.

Decision gravity. Build the routing engine (or buy a Maps API like Google Directions/Mapbox) early on as buy; switching to in-house is a later, reversible swap behind the ETA service interface. Pricing and ETA accuracy directly affect trust, so measure ETA error (p50 and p90 minutes) per city.

Everyday analogy. A GPS app that learns that the highway at 6 pm is slower than the map's speed limit.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling a Maps API per candidate per request (cost and latency explode).
  • Ignoring live traffic.
  • Reporting ETA without saying how it is measured for accuracy.

Location ingestion and the live map

Driver app: sends a ping every 4 s (every 1 s when on trip), batches if the network is bad. Gateway: MQTT, gRPC stream or WebSocket; one gateway box can hold ~100k to 500k idle connections. For 5M drivers, plan about 30 to 50 gateways plus spare.

For the rider's map, the trip service subscribes the rider's session to its driver's pings; gateway pushes driver_moved events every 2 to 4 s, and the client interpolates between points so the car glides.

Reduce load with adaptive frequency (idle driver parked: every 30 s; moving fast: every 2 s) and delta encoding. Dropping a ping is harmless; seq handles out-of-order arrival.

Industry example. Uber's driver app uses a persistent push channel and has written about moving location traffic onto protocols that survive poor networks.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: cars on the rider's map freeze and "nearby drivers" shows ghosts. Metric: ping ingest lag in Kafka and age of newest ping per driver. Cause: gateway reconnect storm after a deploy (millions of devices reconnecting at once). Fix: jittered backoff on clients, connection draining, per-region rollout.

Decision gravity. Soft state (positions) is rebuilt from the next ping in seconds, so you do not need replicas of the index to be strongly consistent: lose a shard and it refills in 4 to 10 s. This choice is easily reversible and saves a lot of money.

Everyday analogy. A radar screen refreshed every few seconds: no need to remember old blips.

Common interview traps.

  • Persisting positions with synchronous replication.
  • Not planning for a reconnect storm.
  • Keeping ghost drivers in the index with no staleness expiry (evict if no ping for 30 s).

Surge pricing and supply-demand (brief)

Per H3 cell per minute compute demand = open requests, supply = free drivers; multiplier rises as the ratio exceeds 1. Smooth over time and neighbouring cells so prices do not flicker. Streaming job (Flink/Kafka Streams) writes the multiplier to a cache the estimate API reads. Quote is locked via quoteId so the rider pays what was shown.

Common interview traps.

  • Computing surge at request time from raw data (too slow, flickers).
  • Changing the price between quote and trip.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Separation of ephemeral location traffic from durable trip state, with different stores.
  • Geo index choice (geohash vs quadtree vs S2/H3), neighbour-cell handling, cell size reasoning, update cost.
  • Numbers: 1M+ pings/s, why the index fits in memory, shard by city.
  • Matching correctness: no double booking, offer timeouts, ranking by ETA, batched vs greedy.
  • ETA: graph routing plus traffic plus ML correction, caching.
  • Failure thinking: gateway reconnect storm, shard loss, driver loses network mid-trip (trip continues; sync later).
  • Seniors also cover idempotent trip creation, the trip state machine as a saga with payment, regional isolation, and cost of storing traces.

Common interview traps.

  • Starting with a database schema instead of the geo problem.
  • Never mentioning consistency requirements on assignment.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Two systems: lossy high-volume location (in-memory geo index, sharded by city) and low-volume correct trips (durable DB, state machine).
  • 5M drivers pinging every 4 s is about 1.25M writes/s, but the live index is only about 500 MB; shard by geography.
  • Geo index with geohash, quadtree or H3 cells: query the rider's cell plus neighbours; pick cell size for 10 to 50 drivers.
  • Match by ETA, not distance; protect against double booking with a single owner and compare-and-set; use offer TTLs; batch matching helps in dense areas.
  • ETA = routing on a preprocessed road graph, live traffic from driver probes, ML correction, and cell-to-cell caching.
  • Design for reconnect storms, stale drivers, idempotent trip creation and regional isolation.

questions.promptHtml: Why would you store live driver locations and trips in two different systems for a ride-hailing service?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The first design decision is recognising two workloads with opposite needs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Driver locations are a huge, lossy, short-lived firehose: millions of pings per second where losing one is harmless because the next arrives in 4 seconds. Trips are low volume but must be correct and durable: no double assignment, no lost payment. So locations go to an in-memory geo index sharded by city, and trips go to a transactional database with a state machine. Putting both in one SQL table would push a million writes per second through the database that guards your money.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Driver ping  -> Location gateway -> Geo index (RAM, soft state, lossy OK)
                                  -> Kafka -> cold trace store (30-day TTL)
Trip request -> Trip service -> Trip DB (ACID, durable, state machine)

Soft state means a lost shard refills from the next pings in 4 to 10 s, so no synchronous replication. Hard state means every transition (REQUESTED to OFFERED to ACCEPTED) is a compare-and-set in a durable store. Different durability, different consistency, different cost per write.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• One table for positions and trips.
  • Persisting each ping with synchronous replication.
  • Forgetting to ask scope (pool, scheduled rides, surge).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What exactly needs strong consistency? -> Only driver assignment (one trip per driver, one driver per trip).
  2. Do you store every ping? -> Not in the transactional DB; sample for trip history, send raw to cheap cold storage.
  3. How big is the live index? -> 5M drivers x ~100 B = about 500 MB; tiny.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use Cassandra for locations". Senior: names the split by durability and consistency, and sizes the index.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that wrote GPS into the trip DB took out bookings during a surge night because ping writes starved transactions.

questions.promptHtml: Compare geohash, quadtree and H3 for finding drivers near a rider. What goes wrong at cell boundaries?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Geo indexing is the core of the problem; the signal is knowing edge effects and cell sizing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A geo index buckets the earth into cells so "who is near me" is a lookup of my cell plus neighbours instead of a scan. Geohash interleaves lat/lng bits into a base-32 string; same prefix means same rectangle, simple and in Redis GEO, but rectangles distort and two close points can have different prefixes. A quadtree splits a cell when it holds more than N drivers, so it adapts to density but needs rebalancing as drivers move. H3 uses hexagons with equidistant neighbours, so a k-ring query is uniform. Whatever I pick, I query the rider's cell and its neighbours, because the nearest driver may be 10 m away in the next cell.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Geohash precision 6  ~ 1.2 km x 0.6 km
H3 res 8 edge ~460 m, res 9 edge ~175 m
Choose resolution so an average cell holds 10-50 drivers.
Lookup: cell(rider) + k-ring(k=1 or 2) -> candidate set -> rank by ETA

Update: ping arrives, compute the new cell; if unchanged (about 90 percent of pings) overwrite lat/lng; otherwise remove from old cell and add to new in one shard operation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
List<String> candidates(double lat, double lng, int k) {
    long center = h3.latLngToCell(lat, lng, 8);          // H3 Java binding; verify API for your version
    List<Long> cells = h3.gridDisk(center, k);
    List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
    for (long c : cells) out.addAll(cellToDrivers.getOrDefault(c, Set.of()));
    return out;
}
fun candidates(lat: Double, lng: Double, k: Int): List<String> {
    val center = h3.latLngToCell(lat, lng, 8)            // verify API for your version
    return h3.gridDisk(center, k).flatMap { cellToDrivers[it].orEmpty() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Searching only the rider's own cell.
  • Straight-line radius across a river.
  • Cells so large that hot downtown cells hold thousands of drivers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why hexagons? -> Every neighbour is the same distance away, so rings are uniform.
  2. Redis GEOSEARCH? -> About 1 ms, about 100k writes/s per node, fine for a first product, then custom sharded service.
  3. Is the cell scheme reversible? -> No: shard boundaries and stored cell ids depend on it, so it is a one-way door.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use geohash". Senior: boundary handling, cell sizing for drivers per cell, density adaptivity, one-way-door cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Missing neighbour-cell lookups made drivers "disappear" for riders standing on a cell boundary.

questions.contextHtml: You are sizing the location tier for 5M drivers online at peak, one ping per 4 s while idle, one per 1 s on trip (assume 20 percent on trip). A candidate answer says "use Redis GEO, one cluster". Ping is 40 B payload, about 100 B on the wire. A gateway holds about 150k connections.
questions.promptHtml: Do the numbers, say how many gateways and index shards you need, and challenge the one-cluster plan.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Averages with no peak, or "Redis handles it" without per-node limits.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Peak versus average? One city or global? Is every ping stored?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; compute.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Writes dominate: 4M idle at 0.25/s = 1M/s plus 1M on trip at 1/s = 1M/s, so about 2M writes/s at peak (the base 1.25M/s case is 5M/4 s). Bandwidth 2M x 100 B = 200 MB/s ingress.
  4. How I'd verify each: Benchmark one index shard at, say, 50-100k updates/s; connection test one gateway at 150k.
  5. Root cause: n/a. Gateways: 5M / 150k = about 34, plan 50 with headroom. Index shards: 2M / 50k per shard (50 percent utilisation) = 40 shards, partitioned by city or cell range. Memory is only 500 MB, so memory does not drive the count; write rate does.
  6. Fix: Shard by geography (city or cell range), not driver id, so "who is near me" hits one shard. Raw pings to Kafka then cold store with a 30-day TTL; history sampled to 1 point per 10 s. Adaptive ping rate (parked driver every 30 s) cuts load 30 to 50 percent.
  7. Prevention: Per-shard ingest lag, age of newest ping per driver, load tests at 1.5x peak.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: One Redis cluster at 100k ops/s per node needs 20+ primaries anyway and cross-slot geo queries get awkward; I would not persist pings synchronously.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Storage if every ping is kept? -> 1.25M x 40 B x 86,400 = about 4 TB/day; hence cold TTL.
  • Can delta encoding help? -> Yes, smaller payloads, but writes/s stay the same.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sizing based on 2 pings/min per driver was off by 8x once on-trip drivers pinged every second.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: No per-node limits.
  • Hire: Writes/s, bandwidth, gateway and shard counts.
  • Strong hire: Adaptive ping rate, cold storage TTL, geography sharding rationale.

questions.contextHtml:
Support reports that two riders were offered the same driver in the same second, and one driver app showed two offers. The matching service runs 8 workers. Code under review:

// per-driver state lives in a shared in-memory map on the shard
boolean tryOffer(String driverId, String tripId) {
    Driver d = drivers.get(driverId);
    if (d.status == Status.AVAILABLE) {
        d.status = Status.OFFERED;
        d.tripId = tripId;
        push(driverId, tripId);
        return true;
    }
    return false;
}

Kotlin equivalent:

fun tryOffer(driverId: String, tripId: String): Boolean {
    val d = drivers[driverId]!!
    if (d.status == Status.AVAILABLE) { d.status = Status.OFFERED; d.tripId = tripId; push(driverId, tripId); return true }
    return false
}
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, and how do you make assignment safe without a global lock?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add synchronized everywhere" or a distributed lock service for every offer.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a driver's state owned by exactly one shard? Is there an offer timeout? Is state also persisted?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route all matching calls for a driver through the owning shard and serialise per driver.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Check-then-act race: two workers read AVAILABLE, both write OFFERED. Also no offer TTL, so a stuck OFFERED never reverts.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add a race test with two threads on one driver; log offers per driver per second.
  5. Root cause: The read and write are not atomic; the invariant "one offer per driver" is not enforced by the state change.
  6. Fix: Languages: Java, Kotlin
Languages: Java · Kotlin
boolean tryOffer(String driverId, String tripId, long now) {
    DriverState cur = states.get(driverId);
    if (cur == null || cur.status != Status.AVAILABLE) return false;
    DriverState next = new DriverState(Status.OFFERED, tripId, now + 15_000);
    return states.replace(driverId, cur, next);   // compare-and-set; false means someone else won
}
fun tryOffer(driverId: String, tripId: String, now: Long): Boolean {
    val cur = states[driverId] ?: return false
    if (cur.status != Status.AVAILABLE) return false
    return states.replace(driverId, cur, DriverState(Status.OFFERED, tripId, now + 15_000))
}

(DriverState must be an immutable value with equals.) Push the offer only when the CAS succeeds; a timer or lazy check reverts expired offers to AVAILABLE. In a database version it is UPDATE ... WHERE status='AVAILABLE' and check 0 rows. 7. Prevention: Concurrency test in CI, invariant metric "drivers with more than one open offer = 0". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a distributed lock service per offer; single ownership of driver state by a shard is simpler and faster.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Shard failover mid-offer? -> State is soft; offer TTL expires and the trip re-matches; accept 409 if the driver already took a different trip.
  • Why include the trip id? -> The accept call must match the offer, or a late accept from an old offer would steal the driver.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Two riders were told the same car was coming; both cancelled and the company paid cancellation credits for a week until the check-then-act got replaced by CAS.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Global lock.
  • Hire: CAS on single owner, offer TTL.
  • Strong hire: Test and invariant metric, failover behaviour, accept validated against offer.

questions.contextHtml:
At 18:02 a gateway deploy restarts all 40 location gateways in one wave. Within a minute riders see cars frozen on the map and "nearby drivers" shows cars that left 10 minutes ago. Metrics:

gateway connections        4.9M -> 0.3M -> 4.6M (over 6 min)
kafka ping ingest lag      0 s -> 95 s
newest ping age p50        4 s -> 71 s
location shard CPU         40% -> 97%

The CDN and API gateway look healthy; a recent change reduced the staleness TTL to 5 minutes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds shard capacity; ignores client behaviour and ghost drivers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did clients retry immediately? Is TLS handshake CPU the bottleneck? How is staleness evicted?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause rollout, shed load by rate-limiting new connections per gateway, scale gateways, temporarily mark drivers with stale pings as unavailable for matching.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) synchronised reconnect storm with no jitter; (b) shard CPU from re-inserting 5M drivers; (c) Kafka backlog; (d) a network issue (unlikely: recovery tracked the reconnect curve).
  4. How I'd verify each: Connection accept rate, client retry logs, TLS handshake CPU, per-shard update rate, age of newest ping per driver.
  5. Root cause: Deploying every gateway at once dropped 5M connections; devices reconnected simultaneously, saturating handshakes and shards, while stale entries stayed searchable because the TTL was 5 minutes.
  6. Fix: Jittered exponential backoff on clients, connection draining and rolling deploys by 5 percent waves per region, resumable sessions to avoid full re-registration, evict drivers with no ping for 30 s (not 5 minutes) from the match index.
  7. Prevention: Deploy canary by region, game day that kills a gateway tier, alerts on newest-ping age and accept rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A 30 s TTL risks flicker on bad networks; use hysteresis (mark unavailable at 30 s, delete at 2 min). I would not make the index durable to survive it: soft state refills in seconds.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just overprovision? -> The peak of a synchronised storm is bursty, 10x the steady rate; backoff costs less than capacity.
  • Trip in progress and connection drops? -> The trip continues; the driver app buffers locations and syncs on reconnect.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A routine certificate rotation restarted a gateway fleet at once; recovery took 12 minutes, of which the deploy itself was 20 seconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Scales shards only.
  • Hire: Identifies reconnect storm and adds jitter and rolling deploy.
  • Strong hire: Stale-driver eviction with hysteresis, drain, canary and correct soft-state reasoning.

questions.contextHtml: Matching queries about 5,000 nearby searches per second at peak. For each, the service calls a third-party Directions API for the top 10 candidates. Assume list price of 5 USD per 1,000 calls (verify current pricing). p99 request-to-offer is 7.8 s against a 5 s target; the vendor p95 is 220 ms per call and calls are made serially.
questions.promptHtml: What is the daily cost ceiling and how do you restructure ETA computation?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Negotiates a price or parallelises all 10 calls and keeps the spend.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which ETAs are for quotes versus final matching? Do we have our own probe data? What accuracy gap is tolerable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce candidates to the top 3 by straight-line distance and parallelise those 3; cache coarse results.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Serial vendor calls dominate latency (10 x 220 ms = 2.2 s, plus retries); cost scales with requests x candidates.
  4. How I'd verify each: Trace spans per vendor call, call count per match, cache hit ratio.
  5. Root cause: 5,000 x 10 = 50,000 calls/s; at 5 USD per 1,000 that is 250 USD/s, about 21.6 million USD per day if sustained at peak, far above any average (still millions). No cache and no staging of cheap versus exact estimates.
  6. Fix: Two stages: (1) cell-to-cell ETA cache keyed by (origin H3 cell, dest H3 cell, time bucket) with a 1 to 5 minute TTL for quotes and candidate ranking; (2) exact routing only for the final 3 candidates. Build an in-house routing engine on a preprocessed graph (contraction hierarchies, sub-millisecond to few ms per query) with live traffic from driver probes, behind the same ETA interface; keep the vendor as fallback. An ML model corrects the residual error.
  7. Prevention: Cost per match dashboard, ETA error metrics per city (p50 and p90 minutes), budget alerts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not build the routing engine on day one: buy first, swap later behind an interface (reversible). I would not trust cached ETAs for the final driver pick in congested areas.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What cache hit rate do you expect? -> High in dense cities for repeated cell pairs; measure per city, verify with traffic.
  • Accuracy complaints? -> Compare predicted versus actual pickup time per segment of the day and retrain the correction model.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch with per-candidate vendor calls produced an invoice that exceeded the revenue of the city it served.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Parallel calls only.
  • Hire: Cost math and two-stage ETA with cache.
  • Strong hire: In-house routing plan behind an interface, accuracy metrics, fallback strategy.

questions.contextHtml: A concert ends at 23:00 and 25,000 riders open the app within five minutes at one stadium, where about 2,500 drivers are within 3 km. The shard that owns that geography is at 100 percent CPU; match latency p95 goes to 40 s, and drivers are offered rides they decline because pickups are far from the gate. Greedy sequential matching assigns each rider the nearest driver.
questions.promptHtml: What changes in the architecture and the matching policy?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more shards" without recognising the problem is one hot geography.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the event planned (calendar known)? Is surge/pricing allowed to shape demand? Are pickup zones allowed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Split the hot cells at a finer H3 resolution and move them to dedicated shards; shed non-essential work (analytics) on that shard.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) one cell owns too many drivers and requests; (b) greedy matching steals drivers from riders who need them more; (c) ETA service saturated.
  4. How I'd verify each: Requests and drivers per cell, per-shard CPU, match latency by cell, decline rate.
  5. Root cause: Sharding by geography concentrates hot spots; greedy per-request matching under extreme density produces poor global assignment.
  6. Fix: Batched matching: every 2 s collect open requests and free drivers in the zone and solve an assignment problem (min total pickup time, Hungarian or min-cost flow, approximations for scale). Define stadium pickup zones so riders walk to a gathering point, raising supply density per cell. Surge multiplier per cell smoothed over neighbours. Pre-scale and pre-split for known events from the venue calendar.
  7. Prevention: Load test with a synthetic hotspot, auto split of cells whose load passes a threshold.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Batching adds up to 2 s of wait; only worth it in dense zones, so keep greedy elsewhere (policy change, reversible). I would not re-shard globally; the sharding key is a one-way door and the issue is local.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not nearest-first? -> It can assign a driver to a rider 100 m closer while another rider has no other option.
  • Cell borders? -> Overlapping lookup cells (k-ring) so candidates across the border are included.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A stadium night produced the highest cancellation rate of the quarter; the fix was gathering points plus batched matching, not hardware.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: More servers.
  • Hire: Cell splitting and batched assignment.
  • Strong hire: Pickup zones, calendar pre-scaling, local policy change, awareness of one-way-door sharding.

questions.contextHtml: The system started with geohash precision 6 cells keyed in every shard, offer, and analytics table. Cells near the equator are fine but rectangles distort, boundary misses cause "no cars nearby" complaints, and the team wants H3 resolution 8. 120 cities run in production; you cannot take downtime and surge pricing, matching and analytics all read cell ids.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the migration and say what you refuse to change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Write a script to convert ids" with no dual-run or rollback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which consumers depend on cell ids (surge, analytics, ML features)? Are cells persisted long-term? Is the city shard boundary separate from cell choice?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the immediate boundary bug with a neighbour-cell lookup in geohash while the migration is planned.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: stale data in two schemes; surge mismatch; analytics history breaking.
  4. How I'd verify each: Shadow queries: for sampled requests compare candidate sets from both indexes; compare average match ETA.
  5. Root cause: Cell id is used as a key everywhere; it is a one-way door.
  6. Fix (plan): Keep city as the shard key (unchanged). Add an H3 index beside the geohash index in the location service; both updated from the same ping (dual-write in memory, cheap). Shadow-read H3 for matching, log the difference. Roll out per city starting with a small one; for each city flip matching to H3, then surge to H3 cells computed from the same stream. Keep a stored (geohash, h3) mapping for history analytics. After a stable month remove geohash writes.
  7. Prevention: Per-city dashboard with candidates found, match latency, offer acceptance, plus a one-flag rollback.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Memory doubles temporarily for the second index (only about 500 MB total, so cheap). I would not rewrite historical analytics; I would map old to new at query time.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not convert ids by formula? -> Geohash rectangles and H3 hexagons do not nest; there is no exact mapping.
  • A city flips and complaints rise? -> Flag back; continue shadow reads to understand.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration that switched all cities at once found a resolution mismatch only in a dense city, where cells held 400 drivers and match latency tripled.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Script conversion.
  • Hire: Dual index, shadow read, city-by-city flip.
  • Strong hire: Keeps shard key stable, maps history, cell-density check per city, rollback.
